nameStory: This little armored critter is named after Heinrich Rathke, a 19th-century German zoologist who made important discoveries about animal development. Rathke studied many small invertebrates, and having this common woodlouse bear his name honors his contributions to understanding these often-overlooked creatures.
description: Rathke's woodlouse is a small, oval-shaped crustacean that looks like a tiny armadillo. These grayish creatures are about the size of a large pill bug, with segmented bodies covered in armor-like plates. Unlike their famous pill bug cousins, Rathke's woodlice cannot roll into a perfect ball when threatened. You'll often find them scurrying under logs, rocks, or leaf litter where they feed on decaying plant matter.

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Oval and flattened with a distinctly segmented appearance - you can clearly count the individual armor-like plates across the back

idTips.label: Rolling ability
idTips.description: Cannot roll into a complete ball when disturbed - they may curl slightly but always leave gaps, unlike pill bugs

idTips.label: Color pattern
idTips.description: Mottled gray to brownish-gray with a somewhat rough, bumpy texture that feels dry to the touch

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Two pairs of antennae with the outer pair being noticeably longer and more prominent

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Scurries quickly in a side-to-side motion when uncovered, much faster than the slower pill bugs

idTips.label: Habitat preference
idTips.description: Found in drier microhabitats than most woodlice - often under bark or in leaf litter rather than soggy soil

habitat: Look for Rathke's woodlice in relatively dry spots under logs, loose bark, stone walls, and deep leaf litter throughout New England's forests and suburban areas. They prefer slightly drier conditions than many other woodlice, often hiding in the spaces between stacked firewood or under the loose bark of dead trees. You'll find them from sea level up into the mountains, especially in mixed hardwood and coniferous forests.

seasonality.spring: Active as temperatures warm, often found under logs and stones as they emerge from winter hiding spots. Look for them during the first warm, humid days.
seasonality.summer: Most active during humid nights and early mornings. Check under bark and in compost piles where they're feeding and reproducing.
seasonality.fall: Very active as they prepare for winter, often gathering in groups under protective cover. This is when you're most likely to find multiple individuals together.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep under logs, bark, and stone foundations where they remain sluggish but alive. Only active during unusual warm spells.

funFact: Despite living on land and breathing air, Rathke's woodlice are actually more closely related to lobsters and crabs than to any insect - they're terrestrial crustaceans that still need moisture to breathe through gill-like structures!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with common pill bugs (roly-polies), but Rathke's woodlice can't roll into a tight ball and are generally more active and faster-moving. Memory trick: 'Rathke's can't make a perfect circle' - they always leave gaps when they try to curl up.
contextualKnowledge: Many people call all small gray creatures under logs 'pill bugs' or 'roly-polies,' but true pill bugs belong to a different family entirely. Rathke's woodlice represent one of several woodlouse species that have successfully made the leap from ocean to land, though they still require some moisture to survive.
compareHints: Since Rathke's woodlouse is the only Trachelipus species commonly found in New England, compare it with the more familiar common pill bug (Armadillidium vulgare). Rathke's woodlice are generally more elongated, faster-moving, and prefer slightly drier conditions than pill bugs. They also have a more mottled appearance and cannot achieve the perfect sphere that pill bugs are famous for.
